title: Justice Will Prevail; It Certainly Will!
translatorNote: This translation is intended to carry Kalaignar's voice into clear, contemporary English rather than recast the letter as literary or academic prose. It preserves the source's argument, political directness, rhetorical questions, repetition, irony, factual detail, and paragraph order. Names, dates, figures, quotations, and intentional English expressions are retained. Where Tamil idiom cannot be reproduced literally without sounding unnatural, the English follows its sense and rhetorical force without adding claims absent from the source. The original Tamil is reproduced in full below the translation and remains the authoritative text. `Udanpirappē` is retained in Tamil transliteration rather than flattened into “brother,” “sister,” or “comrade.” Literally evoking “one born alongside me,” Kalaignar uses it as a distinctive address of shared identity, equality, affection, and solidarity within the movement.
paragraphs: I write this letter with a single resolve: whatever difficulty may arise, I am prepared to face it. The reason is my unshakable faith that justice must stand.

The disproportionate-assets case against Jayalalithaa is being heard in the Special Court in Bengaluru. Mr Bhavani Singh had been appearing for the State as the prosecutor against her. Before him, that position was held by Mr Acharya.

When Acharya was the public prosecutor, numerous complaints were made against him by Jayalalithaa's side. While the BJP was in power in Karnataka, a powerful group from Chennai went to Bengaluru and camped there. As a result, Acharya, with a heavy heart and after openly expressing his distress, sought to withdraw from the case itself. When Special Public Prosecutor B.V. Acharya sent his resignation to the Chief Justice of the Karnataka High Court, the then Chief Justice, Mr Vikramajit Sen, did not accept it. After he was elevated to the Supreme Court, Mr Sridhar Rao became Acting Chief Justice and immediately accepted Acharya's resignation.

After Acharya left, Karnataka appointed Bhavani Singh as the public prosecutor to argue against Jayalalithaa. Yet his conduct repeatedly favoured the accused. Once the examination of Jayalalithaa's witnesses had ended, the prosecutor should have begun the State's arguments. Instead, Jayalalithaa's counsel, P. Kumar, began presenting his arguments, while the public prosecutor simply looked on.

When the matter came before the Supreme Court, senior counsel Vahanvati, appearing for Karnataka, pointed out that the Karnataka Government had never recommended Bhavani Singh for appointment. The State had submitted the names of four other advocates and suggested that the Chief Justice of the Karnataka High Court appoint one of them.

At that time Karnataka had an Acting Chief Justice. It was he who had immediately accepted the resignation of Acharya, the earlier public prosecutor in this case. Yet instead of selecting one of the four advocates already recommended by the Government, the Acting Chief Justice independently appointed Bhavani Singh.

After Nallamma Naidu, the investigating officer in the case, the investigation was handled by DSP Sambandam. He later appeared as a witness supporting the accused. Even then Bhavani Singh raised no objection. If an investigating officer is to be examined as a witness in the very same case, the court itself must summon him. Even that minimum procedure was not followed. DSP Sambandam was secretly brought in as the final witness—the ninety-ninth witness—and made to testify.

This Anti-Corruption Department officer was examined as a defence witness and was permitted to refer to documentary evidence in support of the accused. It is said that he did not even obtain proper permission from his superiors before giving such evidence. The public prosecutor, who should have objected to all this, remained silent, and the judge allowed it.

This was the same officer who had bypassed the public prosecutor and earlier written directly to the Special Judge seeking a reinvestigation of the case. On our petition, the Karnataka High Court rejected DSP Sambandam's request and censured him as an investigating officer acting under the instructions of the present Chief Minister of Tamil Nadu, Selvi Jayalalithaa.

Soon after taking charge, Bhavani Singh filed a petition on 28 February 2013 asking for two months to study the 259 prosecution witnesses and thousands of documentary exhibits. To this day, the Special Court has issued no order on that petition. The time he requested was not granted, and he did not appeal to the High Court.

Only after witnessing all this did the DMK petition the Special Court for permission to assist the prosecution and argue against Jayalalithaa. Judge Balakrishna ruled that we could submit written views but would not be permitted to argue. There has likewise been no answer to our request that former investigating officer Nallamma Naidu be examined.

The seized jewels that form important documentary and material evidence in this case are kept in the vault of the Reserve Bank in Chennai. During the trial, those jewels should have been brought under the court's custody. They have not been brought even now. Before final arguments began, the Special Court issued no order directing that the jewels be produced. Yet the judge appeared eager to pronounce judgment before bringing them to court and examining them—as though he wished to deliver the verdict before his retirement. Judgment cannot properly be delivered without producing and inspecting the jewels in court.

On 23 August 2013, our General Secretary, Perasiriyar, filed a petition in the Karnataka High Court seeking the removal of Bhavani Singh. On 26 August, Justice Bopanna issued notice to the Karnataka Law Department. When the Supreme Court transferred the case to the Bengaluru Special Court, it had directed the Karnataka High Court to ensure a fair trial. That is why the High Court sent notice to the State Government. On that very day, Karnataka ordered Bhavani Singh's removal.

Although the State Government had removed him on the 26th, Bhavani Singh appeared before the Special Court on the 27th and pressed on with his arguments. While he was arguing, the judge learnt that the State had removed him. The judge stopped proceedings and went to his chamber. Bhavani Singh then left the courtroom and held consultations with AIADMK lawyers. What an astonishing sight! Have we not read the story of the tiger and the deer drinking water together? In the same way, the lawyers for the accused and the lawyer who was supposed to oppose them gathered for consultation in the Bengaluru Special Court.

Had Karnataka not removed Bhavani Singh, he would have announced on the 27th itself that he had completed the prosecution's arguments, and the judge would have fixed a date for judgment. From the day the case was transferred to Karnataka, the accused had prolonged it by filing petition after petition. But after Mr Balakrishna became Special Judge, they began making every effort to finish the case quickly. That explains why the judge, without even granting the public prosecutor's request for two months, acted with urgency to pronounce judgment before his retirement on 30 September.

The accused had originally sought to examine 133 defence witnesses. They suddenly reduced their list after examining only ninety-nine. Even those ninety-nine witnesses were not properly cross-examined by public prosecutor Bhavani Singh.

Although the defence submitted important documents as “Xerox” copies, the Special Judge accepted them without objection. This violated the rule that original documents must be produced. The public prosecutor, who should have objected to the acceptance of Xerox copies, showed no concern.

After Karnataka removed Bhavani Singh, he announced on the 28th that he would approach the Supreme Court against his dismissal. On the 29th, Jayalalithaa herself filed a petition in the Supreme Court claiming that the removal of the public prosecutor was unjust. What a spectacle! The accused went to the Supreme Court to object to the replacement of the lawyer appearing against her. Senior lawyers in Delhi are said to have laughed to themselves at the strange sight of an accused challenging the removal of the opposing prosecutor.

The Supreme Court ordered Jayalalithaa's petition to be heard on the 30th. It refused her request for an interim stay on Karnataka's removal of Bhavani Singh, but also directed that no new prosecutor be appointed in the meantime and issued notice seeking the State Government's response.

When the matter came up on 6 September 2013, counsel for Karnataka told the Supreme Court that Bhavani Singh's appointment itself had not been proper, that the State had therefore decided to withdraw him, and that it was ready to appoint a new prosecutor after consulting the Chief Justice. Accepting this, the judges ordered that a new prosecutor be appointed in consultation with the Chief Justice of the Karnataka High Court.
On 10 September 2013, Karnataka's Law Secretary wrote directly to Bhavani Singh. The letter specifically stated:

As the Government of Karnataka was of the view that your appointment was not made in accordance with the directions issued by the Supreme Court in that the requirement of consultation has not been complied with, the Government withdrew your appointment..... In the circumstances the Government is of the view that it would be appropriate that pending consideration of the matter by Hon’ble the Chief Justice, you do not insist upon appearing before the Court in the aforesaid case as Special Public Prosecutor

In other words, the Karnataka Government wrote that his appointment had been withdrawn because it had not been made in accordance with the Supreme Court's directions and the required consultation had not taken place; and that, while the matter of appointing a new prosecutor was pending before the Chief Justice, he should not insist on appearing as Special Public Prosecutor.

Once Karnataka stated this unambiguously on the 10th, instead of Bhavani Singh deciding what he should do, Jayalalithaa's side decided for him. At about one o'clock this afternoon, 13 September 2013, Jayalalithaa filed a petition in the Supreme Court seeking an interim stay on Karnataka's letter directing Bhavani Singh not to appear in the case.

Bhavani Singh is the public prosecutor appointed by the State to argue against Jayalalithaa. Why is Jayalalithaa so desperate that he alone must continue? The Supreme Court has accepted her request and granted an interim stay on Karnataka's letter to Bhavani Singh. What argument did Jayalalithaa's side advance? I shall write about that later.

Because of the Supreme Court's interim order, the case is due to come before the Special Court on the 17th. Meanwhile, the DMK's case in the Karnataka High Court seeking to prevent Bhavani Singh from appearing is to be heard on the 16th.

Special Judge Balakrishna is due to retire on the 30th of this month. The accused want judgment before then. The judge too appeared determined to pronounce judgment before retiring. But there is another complication. According to his date of birth, the Special Judge should have retired on the 12th. When retirement falls in the middle of a month, the Government permits an officer to continue until the month's end for pensionary convenience. On that basis, Judge Balakrishna may continue until 30 September. Yet judicial convention is that, after the natural date of retirement, even if he continues until the month's end, he should not deliver major judgments. Therefore, although he may remain in office until the 30th, the truth is that he can no longer pronounce judgment in this case. Whether the Special Judge will proceed despite this remains a question.

Perarignar Anna wrote the celebrated play Needhi Devan Mayakkam—The Bewilderment of the God of Justice—and acted in it himself. In this disproportionate-assets case too, will the god of justice become bewildered, or will he stand upright? Even if the god of justice is made to lose his balance, I have placed before the true judges—the people of Tamil Nadu—the circumstances surrounding the final stage of this case.
With affection, M.K. 14 September 2013
